Q1. Which of the following modeling choices is most reasonable?
A. Model a runner’s swinging foot as a point mass when computing the torque
about the ankle during a stride.
This is a poor approximation because torque during a stride depends on how mass is distributed
along the foot, not just its total mass at a point.
B. Model a city bus as a point mass when estimating how far it travels along a
highway over several kilometers.
Over kilometer-scale motion, the bus’s size is negligible compared with the displacement, so a
point-mass model is appropriate for position change.
C. You must include air drag explicitly whenever you say you are ignoring air
resistance, because “vacuum” is never realistic.
This confuses physical realism with idealization: using a vacuum model is a standard way to
justify neglecting drag forces.
D. None of the above is correct.
Option B is a valid scale-based approximation, so “none of the above” cannot be correct.

Q2. Which of the following unit-conversion equations is correct?
A. 1 mm = 0.01 m.
This incorrectly treats a millimeter as a centimeter, which is ten times larger.
B. 1 mm = 0.001 m.
A millimeter is one-thousandth of a meter, so the conversion factor is 0.001.
C. 1000 mm = 0.001 m.
This inverts the scale factor, since 1000 mm = 1 m, not 0.001 m.
D. 1 = 0.001.
This drops the units entirely and asserts a false numerical equality.

Q7. A dolphin launches out of the water with speed v0 at an angle θ above the
horizontal (ignore air resistance). What is the dolphin’s speed at the maximum
height?
A. v0.
This ignores that the vertical component decreases to zero at the top, reducing the total speed.
B. v0 sin θ.
This gives the initial vertical component, which becomes zero at maximum height rather than
remaining the speed.
C. v0 cos θ.
At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero while the horizontal component stays v0 cos θ,
so the speed equals v0 cos θ.
D. 0.
Only the vertical component becomes zero at the top; the horizontal component generally
remains nonzero.

product.

Q12. A 3.2 kg cart moving at 1.8 m/s hits a bumper and rebounds at 0.6 m/s
in the opposite direction. The contact time is 0.15 s. What is the magnitude of
the average force exerted on the cart during the collision?
A. 25.6 N.
This corresponds to using ∆v = 1.2 m/s (adding speeds incorrectly) instead of the correct
change from +1.8 to −0.6.
B. 38.4 N.
This often comes from using the correct momentum change but dividing by an incorrect time
such as 0.20 s.
C. 51.2 N.
The momentum change magnitude is m|vf − vi| = 3.2 |−0.6 − 1.8| = 3.2 × 2.4, so Favg =
|∆p|/∆t = 7.68/0.15 = 51.2 N.
D. 76.8 N.
This is the impulse magnitude |∆p| = 7.68 N · s mistakenly reported as a force without dividing
by time.
